content: This updated Cochrane review, originally published in 2012, examines the impact of dietary and exercise interventions, individually or combined, on preventing excessive gestational weight gain (GWG) and associated complications during pregnancy. Excessive GWG is linked to adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes, such as gestational diabetes, hypertension, cesarean delivery, macrosomia, and stillbirth. The review evaluates the effectiveness of these interventions in mitigating these risks. The review included 65 randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with data from 49 trials involving 11,444 women contributing to the quantitative meta-analysis. The interventions studied were categorized into diet-only, exercise-only, and combined diet and exercise approaches, compared to standard care. The findings revealed that these interventions reduced the risk of excessive GWG by an average of 20% (risk ratio [RR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.73 to 0.87). This result was consistent across sensitivity analyses, and the evidence was graded as high quality. All intervention types—low glycemic load diets, supervised or unsupervised exercise, and combined diet and exercise—produced similar reductions in excessive GWG. Women in the intervention groups were more likely to experience lower GWG compared to control groups (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.27). However, there was no significant difference between intervention and control groups regarding the risk of pre-eclampsia (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.16). Maternal hypertension, though not a pre-specified outcome, was reduced in the intervention group (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.96), but this evidence was of low quality. The risk of cesarean delivery was not significantly different between groups (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.03), although a small reduction (5%) in favor of the interventions was suggested. Combined diet and exercise interventions showed a borderline significant reduction in cesarean delivery risk (13% reduction, 95% CI -1% to 25%). There was no clear difference in the risk of preterm birth overall (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.22), but limited evidence suggested that exercise-only interventions might slightly increase the risk of preterm birth. Regarding neonatal outcomes, there was no significant difference in the risk of macrosomia between intervention and control groups (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.02), though a small reduction (7%) in favor of the intervention group was suggested. The largest effect size was observed in the supervised exercise-only group (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.02), which approached statistical significance. High-risk women (e.g., those who were overweight, obese, or had gestational diabetes) receiving combined diet and exercise interventions experienced a 15% reduced risk of macrosomia (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.00). There were no significant differences in other neonatal outcomes, such as shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia, hyperbilirubinemia, or birth trauma. However, infants of high-risk women in the intervention group had a reduced risk of respiratory distress syndrome (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.85). In conclusion, high-quality evidence supports the effectiveness of dietary and exercise interventions, individually or combined, in reducing the risk of excessive GWG. Additional benefits may include a lower risk of cesarean delivery, macrosomia, and neonatal respiratory distress, particularly in high-risk women receiving combined interventions. Maternal hypertension may also be reduced. Exercise appears to play a critical role in weight management during pregnancy, but further research is needed to establish safe and effective guidelines. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries, and the applicability of these findings to low-income settings remains uncertain.
